entry.title: One person can make a difference
entry.content:
In the early days of OpenAI, Sam Altman had a quote painted on the office walls. It comes from Hyman G. Rickover, the admiral known as the father of the nuclear navy, who built the first nuclear-powered submarines:

I believe it is the duty of each of us to act as if the fate of the world depended on him. Admittedly, one man by himself cannot do the job. However, one man can make a difference.

Karen Hao tells the story in Empire of AI (chapter 6). Years later Altman put the same quote, with a few more lines about each person’s “individual and independent capacities”, at the end of a memo to the company. The memo asked for less transparency, at least one impressive demonstration of progress a year, and more seriousness and unity. Under the quote he wrote: “We must put the mission ahead of any individual preferences.”

I like the quote, and I believe it. It is the conviction behind most things worth building, and it is the same thing I argued about who carries progress: a small number of people deciding to act as if it depends on them is how a lot of the future gets made. Rickover is a fair example. A nuclear navy was a state project, but it happened at the pace it did because one difficult man drove it.

What strikes me is the turn in the memo. Rickover’s lines are about the individual: each of us, our own capacities, our own duty. Altman uses them to ask each person to set their own judgement aside for the mission. Both can be true at once, a person can make a difference by joining something larger, but the second reading is the one that makes an organisation dangerous when the mission is as large as the one OpenAI claimed. If everyone acts as if the fate of the world depends on them, someone still has to be allowed to say that the fate of the world is not in fact at stake this quarter.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 6. Hao prints the quote with gender-neutral brackets; the wording above follows the version usually attributed to Rickover.
  • Hyman G. Rickover, attributed to “Thoughts on Man’s Purpose in Life” (1974), as given on Quotepark after Wikiquote. I have not seen the primary text.

entry.title: A billion without a plan
entry.content:
One passage in Karen Hao’s Empire of AI (chapter 5) stays with me more than the chapters around it. In early 2023 a Chinese AI researcher tells her that what OpenAI did could only have happened in Silicon Valley. China has the talent, he says, but no team there would have been given a billion dollars, let alone ten, for an expensive technology without a clear picture of what it would become and what it would be good for. Chinese money followed only after ChatGPT showed there was revenue to be had. Hao takes it one step further: not even Google or DeepMind put open-ended sums into scaling before ChatGPT. It took OpenAI specifically, with its “billionaire origins”, its ideology, and Sam Altman’s fundraising.

Hao uses this against OpenAI’s claim that AGI was inevitable, and she is right on that point. Nothing about it was inevitable. But I read the same fact as a statement about capital. The bet that produced large language models was made before there was a business case, by a small number of people who controlled a lot of money and understood the technology well enough to want it. A committee, a state plan, or a listed company answering to its next quarter would each have asked the question the Chinese researcher’s investors asked, and each would have said no.

That is what concentrated capital is good at. A market economy lets a few people allocate large sums on conviction, and most of those bets fail. The ones that work fund things no consensus process would have chosen. I argue about this often with people who see Silicon Valley’s founders and investors as the problem. I do not think they are villains. They are allocators, some of them unusually good at it, and over the long run economies that reward effective allocation of resources have produced more than economies that plan them. Whether the bet was a good one for everyone else is a separate question, and Hao’s book is mostly about that question.

Two things keep me honest about this:

  • The billionaire origin was more promise than cash. Hao reports (chapter 2) that of the billion dollars pledged at OpenAI’s founding, the lab received only around $130 million, less than $45 million of it from Elon Musk. The pledge bought credibility and talent. The money that paid for scale came later, from Microsoft, a company deciding by very different means.
  • Concentration cuts both ways. The same structure that funds a bet without a plan also leaves the costs of that bet, the data, the labour, the energy, to be decided by the same few people. That is the part of the argument I have not resolved.

The broader argument, about who carries progress and why what they build spreads, is in who carries progress.

Related: allocation is the same act at every scale, a person, a family, and a bank all betting on the future with limited means.

entry.title: Who carries progress
entry.content:
A colleague with a philosophical bent and I had the same argument from opposite ends recently. He distrusts the founders and investors of Silicon Valley, and he holds that the real breakthroughs in science and technology come from academia, and so in the end from the state that funds it. I argued the opposite: progress is carried by people who have to make things work. Entrepreneurs, investors, and companies.

My reasoning goes like this. Someone who has to make a venture survive is selected for the qualities progress needs: being effective, being efficient, daring to try what nobody has asked for. A market does not only reward those qualities once. It trains them, in the people and in the organisations they build, because the ones without them run out of money. An academic can be right for decades without anyone depending on the result. An entrepreneur finds out within a year or two. That feedback loop is the same one I trust when I measure intelligence by what it does rather than by what it knows.

The second half of the argument is the one I care about more. Over the long run, what these people build does not stay with them. Know-how leaks: employees leave and start their own companies, techniques get published or reverse engineered, tools get cheaper until anyone can use them. The sum of many self-interested builders ends up democratising what each of them tried to keep. Large language models are the latest case. A billion dollars bet without a plan became, within a few years, something a single person can run on a laptop.

My colleague has real evidence on his side, and I should say so. The deep learning that OpenAI scaled came out of university labs, Geoffrey Hinton’s in Toronto among them. The web was invented at CERN, a publicly funded laboratory, and Tim Berners-Lee chose to give it away. Where I still disagree is on what counts as the breakthrough. Academia often finds the idea. It usually takes someone with money at risk to turn it into something that reaches everyone, and the Transformer, invented at Google, shows that the line between the two is not as clean as either of us made it sound.

None of this makes me a capitalist in the sense my colleague meant. I am closer to the geolibertarian, or left-libertarian, tradition: Henry George and Silvio Gesell, and in our time Hillel Steiner, Peter Vallentyne, and Philippe Van Parijs. In that tradition you own yourself and what you make, but land and natural resources belong to everyone, and their value should be shared, through a land value tax or a basic income. It fits the argument above. Know-how disperses on its own; land and resources do not, and that is where the sharing has to be designed. And if AI takes us anywhere near post-scarcity, we will have to revisit those designs soon, because the question will no longer be who produces the most, but who owns what is still scarce.

Open threads:

  • Is there a fair test of who carries progress, or does each side count the breakthroughs that suit it?
  • How fast does know-how actually diffuse, and what slows it down: patents, secrecy, scale, compute?
  • What remains scarce when production is cheap, and who should own it?

entry.title: Citizen entrepreneurs
entry.content:
A friend of mine, an enterprise architect at a large Swiss energy group, answers the tumult in between with the observation that the same tools that threaten jobs make citizen entrepreneurs possible. An ordinary person can use AI to identify a business opportunity, use AI to build the business, and use AI to operate it. The barrier was never only money; it was the ten different competences a business needs on day one, and those are now available by the hour. The operating half is already true for infrastructure, where one person can now run what used to take a team, as I argued in How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again. He took his own idea seriously enough to build a business idea factory, a system that generates and evaluates opportunities. About a week before we talked, someone else announced a project with the same shape on Hacker News, which he took as confirmation rather than competition.

I find it the most hopeful reading of the window, and the one with the most work in it. It assumes the capability really is democratised, which I believe, and it assumes people will take it up, which is the part the window is for.
